statements.text: The 2024 Colorado Consumer Protection Act lists deceptive practices in the course of business, vocation or occupation. Examples include knowingly or recklessly passing off goods, services or property as another's, making false representations about source, sponsorship, approval, certification, affiliation or characteristics, and making deceptive representations about geographic origin.

A private action for a listed deceptive trade practice may be brought against a person who engaged in it or caused another to engage in it. Eligible claimants include actual or potential consumers injured by the practice, residential subscribers who receive unlawful telephone solicitation as defined by statute, successors in interest to an actual consumer who purchased the defendant's goods, services or property, and persons injured by the practice in their business or occupation.

The court's private Colorado Consumer Protection Act test required an unfair or deceptive trade practice in the defendant's business, vocation or occupation, significant public impact on actual or potential consumers, injury in fact to a legally protected interest, and causation.

source.citation: Coors v. Security Life of Denver Ins. Co., 91 P.3d 393 (Colo. App. 2003), Part I

statements.text: Subject to the statute's exceptions, a successful individual private action can recover the greatest of actual damages with prejudgment interest, $500, or triple actual damages if clear and convincing evidence establishes bad faith, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees. Interest on actual damages runs from accrual at the greater of 8% annually or the rate in § 13-21-101. Bad faith is fraudulent, willful, knowing or intentional conduct causing injury.
In a certified Colorado Consumer Protection Act class action, a successful plaintiff may recover actual damages, injunctive relief allowed by law, and reasonable attorney fees and costs.

The period is three years from the deceptive act, the last in a series of such acts, or when the consumer discovered or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered the act. The period may be extended by one year if the plaintiff proves that failure to timely commence the action was caused by the defendant engaging in conduct calculated to induce the plaintiff to refrain from or postpone the commencement of the action.
